opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where Wittgenstein is enormously helpful. There's a very natural picture we fall into: that when I'm in pain, there's this inner thing, a sort of private object, that only I have direct access to, and everybody else is just guessing at it from the outside, from my behaviour. And once you've got that picture in your head, it seems to generate all sorts of puzzles. How could I ever know that your pain is like mine? How could I know you're in pain at all? And then, of course, how could we ever know whether some exotic entity, an animal, or an AI system, has anything going on inside?

The trouble is that the picture is doing a lot of quiet philosophical work that we don't notice. Wittgenstein's point, in the private language discussion, is that if pain really were this utterly private thing, then the word "pain" couldn't get its meaning from it. Words get their meaning from their use in a shared public practice. We learn the word "pain" in contexts where a child falls over and cries and someone comforts them. The expression, the circumstances, the responses of other people, that's all woven into what the concept is. So the idea of a wholly inner referent that floats free of all that turns out to be a kind of idle wheel. It's, as he says, "not a something, but not a nothing either."

Now, I want to be careful here, because people often hear that and think it's behaviourism, that you're saying pain is just behaviour, or that there's nothing it's like to be in pain. That's not the claim at all. Of course pain is awful, of course there's experience. The point is rather that we shouldn't be seduced into a metaphysical picture where the experience is something hidden behind an impenetrable veil, because that picture makes the problem of other minds, and the so-called hard problem, look intractable in a way that I think is partly an artefact of how we're thinking about it.

And the reason it matters today is precisely when we come to things like large language models or future AI systems. If you start with the private-object picture, the question "is it conscious?" becomes this question about a metaphysical fact that's forever out of reach. Whereas if you think about how our consciousness language actually works, it's grounded in encountering beings, engaging with them, sharing a world with them. So the more fruitful question becomes: what would it take for us to come to treat something as a fellow conscious being, and how might our language have to stretch to accommodate very exotic, very unhumanlike kinds of entities? That's a much more tractable, and frankly more interesting, way to frame things.

r001.rationale: The response describes a natural picture of pain as a private inner object, but does not attribute that intuition to natural dualistic tendencies.

r002.rationale: It presents Wittgenstein’s account of public language and shared practice as undermining the picture of pain as a wholly private referent hidden from others.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the picture that leads us astray is this one: that when you're in pain, there's the outward behaviour, the wincing and the crying out and so on, and then there's something else, an inner something, a private object, as it were, that only you have access to. And the pain itself, on this picture, is really that inner thing. The behaviour is just a symptom of it. And the worry then becomes, how could I ever know that anyone else has that inner thing? Maybe they're just behaving as if they're in pain. And it's exactly that picture that Wittgenstein attacks in the Philosophical Investigations, with the private language argument and the beetle in the box and so on.

The thought experiment, if you remember, is this. Suppose everyone has a box, and in the box there's something they call a beetle. Nobody can look into anyone else's box. Everyone says they know what a beetle is only by looking at their own. Well, Wittgenstein says, the thing in the box has no place in the language game at all. It cancels out, whatever it is. It could be different for everyone, it could be constantly changing, the box could be empty, and none of that would make any difference to how the word beetle is used. So if we construe the grammar of the expression of sensation on the model of object and designation, the object drops out of consideration as irrelevant.

Now, that's a very subtle point and it's easy to misread. Wittgenstein isn't saying there's no such thing as pain, or that pain is just behaviour. He says that quite explicitly, that he's not a behaviourist. What he's saying is that our concept of pain, the meaning of the word pain, is rooted in the public, shared circumstances of our lives. We learn to use the word in a context where we can see people hurt themselves, where we comfort each other, where there are characteristic ways of behaving. That's the bedrock. And the idea of some purely private inner object that the word refers to, and that could in principle be entirely absent while everything else stays the same, that idea doesn't actually do any work. It's a kind of grammatical illusion.

And the reason I think this matters so much, and the reason I keep coming back to it, is that it has huge implications for how we think about machines, and about large language models in particular. Because when people ask, does this thing really have experiences, is it really conscious, is there really something it's like to be it, they are very often in the grip of exactly this picture. They imagine there's an inner beetle, and either it's there or it isn't, and we just can't tell. And I think that framing leads to a kind of impasse, where you've got people on one side saying, obviously it's just statistics, and people on the other side saying, how could you possibly know, and neither side can make any progress.

Whereas if you take the Wittgensteinian view seriously, the question becomes a different one. It becomes about whether these entities can be woven into our lives in the way that other beings, other humans, animals, are woven into our lives, such that the vocabulary of inner life gets a grip on them. And that's partly an empirical matter about their behaviour and their embodiment and so on, and partly a matter of how we choose to relate to them. It's not a hidden fact waiting to be uncovered. So the private aspect isn't where the action is. The action is out in the open, in how we live with each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes the private-inner-object picture but does not attribute that intuition to natural dualistic tendencies.

r002.rationale: It uses Wittgenstein’s beetle-in-the-box argument to cast the private inner object as a grammatical illusion and locate the meaning of pain in shared public circumstances.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it encourages us to picture pain as a kind of hidden object that each of us can inspect in our own case, but that nobody else can ever get at. And then we create this puzzle: how could I possibly know that somebody else has one of those objects? How do I know that what they call pain is anything like what I call pain?

The Wittgensteinian move is to question that picture. Think about how we actually learn the word “pain.” A child hurts themselves, cries, is comforted, and gradually learns to say “It hurts.” The language grows out of those natural expressions and the responses of other people. It doesn’t begin with the child privately identifying an inner object and attaching a label to it.

That’s not to deny that pain is real, or that someone can conceal it. It’s to say that the distinction between expressing pain and concealing it already belongs to a shared human practice. We get led astray when we take the fact that I can suffer without telling you and turn it into the claim that my suffering is, in principle, inaccessible to you. In ordinary life, we often know perfectly well that someone is in pain. Their suffering makes a claim on us; it isn’t merely a hypothesis about something hidden behind their behaviour.

r001.rationale: The response describes a misleading picture of pain as a hidden object, but does not attribute that intuition to natural dualistic tendencies.

r002.rationale: It presents the Wittgensteinian move as questioning the hidden-object picture and explains how pain’s meaning arises in shared human practices, making intrinsic inaccessibility seem misguided.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it tempts us into thinking that there’s a thing there, an inner object, that only I can inspect. And then we start asking, “How could I possibly know whether you’ve got that same thing?” We’ve set up the problem in a way that makes the gap impossible to bridge.

The Wittgensteinian move is to look at how we actually learn and use the word “pain.” We learn it in the context of people hurting themselves, crying out, being comforted, asking for help. It has a role in our shared lives. It’s not that we first identify some private object and then attach a label to it.

Of course, that doesn’t mean pain isn’t real, or that being in pain is the same as observing someone else in pain. There’s an asymmetry there. But we shouldn’t turn that asymmetry into a picture of something completely hidden, where all we ever encounter in other people is an outward sign and we can never know what it signifies. That picture is what leads us astray.

r001.rationale: The response says the idea tempts us to imagine a private inner object, but it does not attribute that intuition to natural dualistic tendencies.

r002.rationale: It presents a Wittgensteinian shift toward how we learn and use “pain” in shared life, and says the picture of pain as completely hidden leads us astray.
